sources.citation: Ring, Hiram. 2015. A grammar of Pnar. PhD thesis, Nanyang Technological University.
sources.note: Describes Pnar (not Lyngngam): section 2.3.5 'Stress is the main means of distinguishing word boundaries in Pnar. The final syllable of a word carries heavier stress than preceding syllables'. Mentions Lyngngam only as a sister language and cites 'Keren Baker, forthcoming' for Lyngngam-area varieties (Maram, Langrin, Remem, Molang, Nongtrai).

sources.citation: Sidwell, Paul. 2014. Proto Khasian: an emerging reconstruction. In Hyslop, Konnerth, Morey & Sarmah (eds.), North East Indian Linguistics 6, 149-163. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics.
sources.note: p. 151 (section 2.1 Word/syllable structure), on Khasian generally: 'Sonorant consonants and/or epenthetic vowels between stop sequences... can create phonetic unstressed initial syllables, but syllabification in such cases is treated as secondary/superficial. Baker (2013) and Ring (2012) do report some examples of contrastive unstressed vowels in Lyngngam and Pnar respectively'; 'Baker (2013:65) describes Lyngngam as having a maximal word structure CVCCVC'. Second-hand report of Baker 2013; implies stress falls on the main (final) syllable of a sesquisyllabic word but never states the positi…

sources.citation: Sidwell, Paul. 2011. Proto Khasian and Khasi-Palaungic. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 4(2): 144-168.
sources.note: Comparative phonology of Khasian; no occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent' in the article (grep of the volume text: the only stress/accent hits are in unrelated Thai and Japanese papers).

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed.) 1904. Linguistic Survey of India, vol. II: Mon-Khmer and Siamese-Chinese families. Lyng-ngam section.
sources.note: Short dialect note ('The Lyng-ngam dialect of Khassi...'): sound correspondences, articles, case prefixes, specimen; no remark on accent or stress.

sources.citation: Konnerth, Morey & Teo (eds.) 2018. North East Indian Linguistics 8 (Mnar phonology paper citing Nagaraja 1996 on Lyngngam).
sources.note: Concerns Mnar (a Khasian variety), not Lyngngam; Lyngngam mentioned only for its inventories after Nagaraja 1996; nothing on Lyngngam stress.

sources.citation: Daladier, Anne. 2015. The counting unit system of Pnar, War, Khasi, Lyngam and its traces in Austroasiatic composite cardinal systems. In Konnerth et al. (eds.), North East Indian Linguistics 7, 179ff. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics.
sources.note: Numerals and counting units (Langkma Lyngam data); nothing on stress. Contributor note says Daladier 'has prepared three grammars of the core varieties of War, Lyngam and Pnar' (unpublished).

sources.citation: Nagaraja, K. S., Paul Sidwell & Simon Greenhill. 2013. A lexicostatistical study of the Khasian languages: Khasi, Pnar, Lyngngam, and War. Mon-Khmer Studies 42: 1-11.
Daladier, Anne. 2011. The group Pnaric-War-Lyngngam and Khasi as a branch of Pnaric. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 4(2): 169-206.
sources.note: Section 3, p. 176: 'There are no major differences in the phonotactics of Pnar, War, Lyngngam and S. Khasi but there are major differences in their intonation systems, Khasi being the most innovative with no or little word accentuation and final accentuation of utterances.' Implies Lyngngam (unlike Khasi) retains word accentuation, but gives no placement rule; rest of the article is lexical/morphological comparison.

sources.citation: Nagaraja, K. S. 1996. The status of Lyngngam. Mon-Khmer Studies 26: 37-50.
sources.note: Section 1 'Phonology' (p. 38) gives only a tentative vowel and consonant inventory plus five remarks on length, barred-i, palatal series, aspirates and fricatives; no mention of stress, accent, tone or syllable prominence anywhere in the 14 pages (scanned grep: zero hits for stress/accent/tone).

sources.citation: Ring, Hiram. 2026. The Khasian languages of Northeast India: between, but not wholly of, South and Southeast Asia. Journal of Burma Studies 30(1): 117-158.

sources.note: The only dedicated phonology of Lyngngam (Glottolog hhtype phonology); Sidwell 2014 cites it (p. 65) for word structure and for contrastive unstressed vowels, so it almost certainly has a stress/prosody section. Not in ANU Open Research or the ANU library catalogue; probably held only by the ANU School of Culture, History and Language or the author/supervisor (Paul Sidwell).
